analysis.one_liner: Lets workers unionize by signing cards instead of an election, with tougher penalties for employers who retaliate.
analysis.headline: 228 of 253 House Democrats cosponsored the bill, but it never received a vote in either chamber before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how workers form unions. If a majority of workers at a workplace sign cards saying they want a union, the National Labor Relations Board would certify the union directly instead of running a secret-ballot election weeks or months later [S2, S3]. If the employer and union cannot agree on a first contract after 90 days of bargaining plus 30 days of mediation, a government arbitration panel would set the contract terms, binding both sides for two years [S2, S3]. It would also speed up federal investigations when employers fire or threaten pro-union workers during an organizing drive, and would double back-pay awards plus add civil penalties up to $20,000 per violation for willful or repeated retaliation [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want to join a union, and existing unions. Under current law an employer can delay an election for months, run an aggressive anti-union campaign in the meantime, and fire union supporters with little real penalty; the bill would certify a union as soon as a majority of workers sign for it, guarantee a route to a first contract through mediation and binding arbitration, and make firing a union supporter cost up to three times the lost pay plus a fine of up to $20,000 per violation [S2, S3].

how_it_helps.text: If a majority of employees in a bargaining unit sign valid authorizations, the NLRB must certify the union without directing an election [S2, S3].

First contracts are forced onto a timeline: bargaining must start within 10 days, after 90 days either side can request federal mediation, and 30 days after that an arbitration board settles the dispute with a decision binding for two years [S3].

Charges that an employer fired, threatened, or coerced workers during an organizing drive or before a first contract get priority investigation, and remedies are strengthened: back pay plus 2 times that amount in liquidated damages, and a civil penalty of up to $20,000 per willful or repeated violation [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially large nonunion companies. They would lose the period between an organizing drive and an election, when they can currently campaign against the union; they would face binding third-party terms on first contracts; and retaliation against union supporters would carry financial penalties that do not exist today [S3]. Supporters of the bill argue these costs fall on employers who currently rely on delay and retaliation; opponents argued the costs would eventually show up in business decisions about where to invest and hire.

drawbacks.text: The card-check process replaces a secret-ballot election: a worker signs a card in front of, or handed to, a union organizer, and the bill removes the later private vote, which critics said leaves room for pressure on workers from either side in the organizing drive [S3].

If bargaining stalls, a government-appointed arbitration panel would impose a contract binding for two years that neither the employer nor the union voted on, setting wages and terms by third-party decision rather than agreement [S3].

The doubled back-pay and up-to-$20,000 penalties apply to any willful or repeated unfair labor practice during organizing, which employers argued would chill legitimate management speech and add litigation risk to ordinary personnel decisions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: federal labor law currently penalizes employers so lightly that firing union supporters can be a rational business decision, and the bill attacks exactly that with priority investigations and triple-damages-plus-fine remedies [S2, S3]. The costs are also real: card-check removes the secret ballot, and mandatory arbitration of first contracts hands wage-setting to a third party in stalled negotiations, which is a genuine change from agreed-upon contracts and a fair target of the objection [S3]. On balance this is a deliberately one-sided shift toward workers after decades in which enforcement favored employers, and how one weighs it depends largely on whether one sees the current election period as a protected choice for workers or a delay window for employers.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee it was referred to never reported it and no chamber ever voted on it; the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 10, 2009 and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S1, S5].
On April 29, 2009 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, and no markup or vote on the bill ever appears in the action history [S5].

With 228 of 253 House Democrats cosponsoring, the bill had a clear House majority on paper, but leadership never brought it to the floor, and the Senate never acted on it before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1, S4, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and the business coalitions that campaigned against the bill are better off: the election-based system, the lengthy pre-election period, and the weak penalties for retaliation all remained in place. Workers hoping the bill would make organizing cheaper to win are left with the status quo.

for.name: George Miller
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA), senior Democrat on the Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a broad list of original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: 228 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it an apparent House majority.

for.name: Organized labor (AFL-CIO and affiliated unions)
for.what_they_did: Made passage of the Employee Free Choice Act their top legislative priority and campaigned publicly for it throughout 2009.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Unified against the bill, so Senate Democratic leaders lacked the 60 votes needed to cut off debate and bring it to a floor vote; the Senate never voted on it.

against.name: Arlen Specter
against.what_they_did: Announced in March 2009 that he would vote against ending debate on the bill, removing the vote Senate supporters were counting on to reach 60.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and allied business groups
against.what_they_did: Ran a large-scale public and lobbying campaign against card-check certification and mandatory arbitration of first contracts.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled a markup; it sat at the subcommittee referral step for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was overwhelmingly Democratic: 228 of 253 House Democrats cosponsored it versus 3 of 178 House Republicans, and Senate Republicans uniformly opposed it.

industries.note: The bill removes the pre-election campaign window, forces first contracts through mediation and binding arbitration, and puts a price tag on firing or threatening union supporters [S3]. Their interest in keeping the current system runs against workers' ability to organize at low cost.

Certification by signed cards, guaranteed first contracts, and tougher remedies would substantially grow membership and bargaining power [S2]. Union gains come from the same mechanism that lowers the cost of organizing for workers.

industries.industry: Union-avoidance consultants and anti-union law firms
industries.note: A large consulting industry sells campaigns to defeat union elections during the pre-election window; card-check certification would eliminate the window those services depend on. Their interest runs against workers who want to organize.
